speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF CANADIAN CITIZENS IN LABRADOR
speechtext:
I should like to reply to a question asked just before Easter by the hon. member for Kootenay West. I have sent the hon. member a copy of my reply, but I should like to give it to the house. His question can be divided into three parts. The first part is:
Are Canadian citizens seeking employment in Labrador required to complete standard form 60 of the United States civil service commission, handed to them by United States army officials?
The answer is as follows: It is presumed that this question refers to the employment of Canadians on Canada-United States mutual defence projects in Labrador. On the construction of these projects, contractors do their own hiring through the national employment offices of the unemployment insurance commission. The contractors use their own application forms.
The United States air force and the United States army corps of engineers also employ Canadians in connection with those defence activities in Labrador which are a United States responsibility. Recruitment of these Canadians is carried out through the national employment offices of the unemployment insurance commission. Since such persons are to be employees of the United States government, the application form used is that of the United States civil service commission.
The second part of the question is:
If so. do these army officials have the final say as to the employment of the applicant?
The answer is as follows: Whether personnel are employed by contractors engaged by the United States army corps of engineers or by the United States air force, the final decision as to the employment of applicants rests with the employer.
The third part of the question is:
Why are Canadian security personnel not used for this purpose?
The answer is as follows: In either case when there are security considerations involved, the security check is the sole responsibility of Canadian security authorities.

The house resumed, from Monday, April 9, consideration of the motion of Hon. W. E. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned last evening I was advocating bilingualism. Continuing now on another very important subject I would like to say a few words on the change of site for the new post office.
Acting on the recommendation of its town planners and chamber of commerce, the city of Quebec had asked the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) to study the possibility of changing the proposed site of the building and to choose instead property at present occupied by the Canadian National Railways. I was shown a model of the building on the original site and on the new proposed site. In my view, if the proposed changes are carried out, they would unquestionably constitute a definite advantage for the city, the Canadian National Railways and the Post Office Department. The project as it was described to me would mean a threefold transfer of property. The government would turn over to the city the present site which it has lately cleared. The city would have previously obtained from the Canadian National Railways the Ste. Anne station in exchange for St. Andre street. It then would transfer to the government the Ste. Anne station site. The three properties cover approximately the same area. After receiving a resolution to this effect from the city of Quebec, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) suspended the execution of the original plan and expressed his willingness to discuss with the civic authorities, at their convenience, the exchange between the city and his department of the property owned by the government at the present time, and that which the city expects to obtain from the Canadian National Railways. I wish to congratulate the minister for his co-operative attitude, and I am confident that the problem will be solved to the satisfaction of all concerned.
The limited time at my disposal does not allow me at the moment to discuss other important problems such as unemployment benefits for seasonal workers, for instance longshoremen, sailors, freight handlers. There is also the question of the Sillery wharf and other matters too numerous to mention in the time at my disposal. However, I shall endeavour to deal with all these questions some other time.
(Text):
I would like to thank you, Mr. Speaker, and the members of this house for your kind attention to my maiden effort.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all may I congratulate the hon. member who has just taken his seat on his maiden speech; and
The Budget-Mr. F. C. Power may I say with very real sincerity that I can extend no more generous wish to him than that he carry out his promise of independence of thought and devotion to the public service which was displayed by his father during so many years in this house. Whatever our political opinions may be, his father, whom we all know affectionately as "Chubby" Power, will always be remembered with high regard by every one of us here as a great parliamentarian.
Naturally the first point I wish to deal with is the subamendment which will be voted on today. It is customary for the Leader of the Opposition to indicate the position of his party in regard to amendments of this kind.
The subamendment before us covers different subjects. With some of the points raised we are in agreement. However, I think I should read the subamendment so we can bear in mind exactly what it is that it is suggested we should support on this occasion. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) states that the following words be added to the amendment:
that it has failed to reduce the burden of sales and income taxes on those in the lower income groups, while continuing to favour privileged interests and those with unearned incomes by maintaining the 20 per cent dividend tax credit and by refusing to impose a tax on capital gains.
The latter part of this amendment may have an appealing sound to those who adopt the policy of "soak the rich" and seek to claim that this is a general political doctrine. It is put forward with the idea that there will be a suggestion that this is an attempt to deal with those having large incomes. The result would be the very opposite. In a country with an expanding income, such as ours, not through the virtues of this government, as the Minister of Finance was careful to point out in his own speech, a tax of this kind would soak the poor. Every small householder whose home increased in value would be taxed under a proposal of this kind, to the extent of that increase in value. Every small farmer whose farm increased in value would be taxed to the extent of that increase under a proposition of this kind.
Moreover, in a period when unhappily there is a great deal of inflation, it might well be that although the figures in dollars gave an apparent increase, there would be no real increase at all or even a net loss in terms of real dollar value. In a country of this kind, expanding as it is, I can think of nothing that would have a more unsatisfactory effect on our economy than an attempt to tax those increases that come as a natural part of the growth and development of the country.

The Budget-Mr. Drew
The rich people, you know, have a habit of being able to deal fairly satisfactorily with problems of this kind. Usually they are able to take care of themselves, particularly under a government which is so closely tied in with big business and is so solicitous of wealth, especially if it is foreign wealth. This government has unquestionably shown great interest in that field. Undoubtedly it has made it easier in a number of ways for those with wealth to meet some of these problems. The people who would be seriously affected by a capital gains tax in Canada would be the small farmers, the small householders and the small property owners generally. It would also discourage initiative at a time when there is so much evidence that we need to encourage initiative in every way possible. We shall certainly vote against a proposal which would produce such an unsatisfactory result.
I intend now to refer to something that has been very much in the press during the past few days, and which I believe is of very direct and immediate concern to every Canadian and everyone in the western world. I am referring to the visit to Great Britain within the next two weeks of Bulganin and Khrushchev. This is not an ordinary visit. This is the first occasion since the Russian revolution in 1917 that the head of the Russian state has come out to visit the western world. This is the first time there has been an opportunity for people in the western world to sit down in their natural surroundings and discuss affairs in this manner. I am not forgetting, of course, the visit of the Russian representatives to Geneva last year, but I recall that that was a broad international conference. The coming conference is to be one of those exchanges between the heads of state, one of those meetings which present unique opportunities for frank, confidential and open discussion of the great issues which concern us all at this time.
We have been told very frequently of the close relationship and the constant exchange of ideas between the governments of Canada and the United Kingdom. It is probably the only visit of this kind that will be made for some time by the heads of the Russian state to one of the great powers of the western world. Only yesterday, in the House of Commons at Westminster, Sir Anthony Eden said that the important problems of Europe would be discussed at this time, it does seem desirable that the Canadian government should indicate some of the subjects it hopes will be discussed in those conferences.
I am not suggesting for one moment that we abdicate in any way our right as a sovereign state to assert our own position through


the ordinary channels; nevertheless here will be discussed at the very top level some of the most immediate problems and it would seem appropriate that the Canadian government express its own opinion as to some of the things that might well be considered in the interests of the western world at this time. It can do so not only by its representations to the government of the United Kingdom, but it will also be able to do so through its own representatives there, who undoubtedly will be afforded an opportunity on this occasion for personal contact with Khrushchev and Bulganin.
I believe that we all welcome the evidence of extended contacts between Russia and the free world, but I sometimes question whether the desire which is naturally in the hearts of every one of us for peace and security does not lead people to strange and unnatural manifestations of that sentiment on some occasions. I find it just a little difficult to understand the sentiments which led people to demonstrate in the way they did at Canterbury cathedral when Malenkov visited it two weeks ago Sunday under the guidance of the red dean. It was only a few days ago that General Serov left London. The friendly gestures which were extended to Mr. Malenkov were not extended to General Serov; in fact General Serov was described as a murderer and butcher, as he is.
The Russian response to that statement or to the opinions which were expressed was to withdraw Serov's name from the list of those who will visit Britain two weeks from now with Khrushchev and Bulganin. But do people forget that these are the employers of Serov, and that if Serov is a butcher and thug and murderer these people are the employers of that butcher, thug and murderer? That at least might be borne in mind before those of us in the western world who want to see friendship extended as much as possible go completely off the deep end in our efforts to convince the representatives of the Soviet empire that we accept their gestures at face value.
I believe these exchanges are good as long as the facts are clearly borne in mind. I believe it will be very good for Khrushchev and Bulganin to see Britain, and I think it would be a good thing if they could see North America, if they could come to Canada and the United States. I would think also it would be a very good thing if the Russians would extend the same facilities to similar persons from the west to visit with equal freedom different parts of Russia, and also make sure that the press of Russia gave the same coverage to those visits as the press of Britain and the free world is giving to the Russians at this time.

Let us keep it all in perspective. Let us hope that our natural desire for friendship and peace will not let the smiles which now constitute the new party line beguile us into forgetfulness of the dreadful reality that has not changed in any way. Let us not forget the millions who have been slaughtered. Let us not forget that these people who employ General Serov as the head of the secret police now have in concentration camps between 12 and 15 million people living under conditions as vile and terrible as those imposed by the nazis in their days of terror. These are things that perhaps it would be wise to bear in mind. It would be wise to bear in mind that nearly as many people as make up the whole population of Canada are now living in those slave camps, placed there without trial of any kind.
Having said that, let us not close the door to hope. Let us not admit that we have abandoned all hope of some rationalization of this terrible situation. But, Mr. Speaker, the remarks I am making now, at a time when this visit is impending, are made in the hope that what is said here may offer suggestions as to thoughts that would properly and appropriately be conveyed to the government of the United Kingdom at this time. In the discussions that take place in London let us hope that in addition to the opportunity for increased contact and good will we also test their good faith. Surely this would be a particularly good time to suggest to the representatives of Russia who are visiting the free world and seeing how we live that nothing will better encourage the free world to believe in their protestations than clear and unquestioned evidence that they are ending religious persecution in the communist states.
There is something more, and something I am inclined to think we have been far too ready to forget. The smiles that undoubtedly will be registered by the newsreel and television cameras during the visit of Khrushchev and Bulganin will not mean very much to some 150 million people who were enslaved by the Russian armies and have not yet been freed. These smiles are not going to mean very much to the people of Poland, of the Ukraine, of Czechoslovakia, of Hungary, Bulgaria, Roumania, the Baltic states or East Germany, where the Russians are exercising control completely contrary to the Potsdam arrangements. These smiles will not offer any encouragement to them unless something more is done.
This is the time to point that out. This is the time to say with frankness and good will, "The best evidence you can give us of your good faith is that you now carry out the undertaking that was implicit in the charter of the United Nations signed at San
The Budget-Mr. Drew Francisco in 1945". I do not know why we are so reluctant to emphasize this point. I do not know why there should be any tendency to say that the Russians would not do it and then not put the argument forward. After all, they are constantly pressing their points. They are constantly talking about colonialism. The same Khrushchev and Bulganin were fairly free in their comments when in India last December. They do not hesitate to condemn the very reasonable exercise of authority that has been extended by the western world in many parts of the world, to the advantage of those countries in the end in almost every case.
Surely the time has come for us to talk about the very worst form of colonialism that has existed in all history. Surely as people sit down and talk to these men it is proper to say, "If you really mean all this then now is the time to agree with us that exactly the same thing be done that was done after the first world war. Agree with us that votes should be taken in the satellite states". Remember, not one of these satellite states joined Russia even by a communist coup except in the case of Czechoslovakia. Every one of these states was overrun by the Russian armies moving forward to attack Germany. They have remained there and imposed their will by force and terror, and still do.
Now is the time to say that if there is good faith, if this is a new deal, if this does represent a new attitude on the part of Russia and an acceptance of moral obligations, then let there be agreement that under the auspices of the United Nations there will be a vote in each one of these countries to decide what kind of government they will have. What reasonable objection could Russia have to such a suggestion? If they say these countries want communism, then let these countries declare it by a vote that is completely free under a committee on which there is Russian representation as well as representation from the west. Surely we can do what was done under the league of nations, and done in different areas. A vote of that kind was taken in the Saar only a few weeks ago under different auspices. This is nothing new. This is a tested method of asserting in practical form the principle that was declared first of all in the covenant of the league of nations in 1919 and later in the charter of the United Nations in 1945. What better subject could there be for discussion than a discussion of the reality that presents itself to us at this time?
Then I come to East Germany. There is no reason why we should perhaps place East Germany in a position of special favour. People have good reason to recall that twice

The Budget-Mr. Drew within the memory of many of us here Germany has sought to dominate the world by military power. Many here in this chamber took their part in stemming the tide of aggression let loose upon the world by different German governments in two world wars.
There are, however, special reasons why we should bear East Germany in mind. This is no academic problem for the university classroom. This is no problem for discussion groups alone. This is the most vital problem affecting the future of our people at this time. For more than a million Canadians what happens to the satellite states is something of deep and immediate concern. These countries now enslaved are the homelands of more than a million of our people here in Canada.
But for every Canadian those countries have a special appeal on the ground of the moral obligations we undertook. Surely this is a time to recall that this country went to war in 1939 because Poland was attacked. We went to war for as high a principle as has ever taken men and women along the road of sacrifice. That principle was the right of every nation to establish its own form of government by its own choice. That principle is now at stake.
But East Germany can be of even greater concern from the practical point of view. There is no use arguing now the right or wrong of what was done. When the western powers agreed to let Western Germany rearm, they not only gained a powerful ally in western Europe but forces were let loose which should be carefully watched. In five years West Germany will be rearmed. In five years West Germany will probably have an army of over one million highly trained men. They will have the latest type of aircraft with all the advantages that have been gained by the inventions of the western world. We know only too well that their armour and their artillery will be of superlative quality.
What a rearmed Western Germany will do five years from now if East Germany has not yet been united to it under such a free vote as I have suggested should be the concern of every one of us at this time. Can anybody be in any doubt as to what is going to happen unless unification takes place before that time? Look at the map of Germany. There are many here who have been in Germany. Those who have been there remember that Berlin is over 100 miles beyond the iron curtain, far into East Germany.
I hear someone opposite say that is a pretty bald statement. It is. Has anyone forgotten what a much weaker Germany did when they invaded the Rhineland before the last world war? Berlin is still the capital of Germany

in the hearts and minds of all Germans. There is no higher obligation of statesmanship at this time than to bring about the unification of both parts of Germany. Otherwise you have two explosive forces kept apart. The situation is like those terrible devices that were placed in ships leaving the United States in the first world war. They were small containers that had at one end one kind of acid and at the other another kind of acid. In between was a plate that would be steadily eaten away. When that plate was eaten away there came the explosion and the fire. Something of the same kind exists in the situation I have described. Hence now is the time to insist that in East Germany and the satellite states the obligations of the United Nations charter to which Russia is a signatory shall be fulfilled.
Only yesterday our minds were called back to the great battle of Vimy. There are many who will remember that dreadful day. There are many who will remember the slaughter on that occasion. It is a good thing that we should remember the price that has been paid for this freedom of ours. It is also wise to remember the dreadful cost of war. At such a time as this it is a good thing not to forget that time is running out. When we watch the smiles of the heads of the Russian state we should also recall that there was a period of sweetness and light before the last world war. I think we all recall that the then prime minister of Canada, the late Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, visited Hitler and came back with the report that he was sure Hitler had no intention of carrying out aggression. That was as late as 1937.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the article you wrote?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh, yes; I wrote an article entitled "Germany prepares for conquest". If you like I will send a copy of it to you. I do not hesitate to recall the fact that I said then that all the evidence was that Germany was preparing for aggression. I am not raising this part of our own history in order to embarrass anyone. I recall that there were others who were equally beguiled by the smiles. I remember that there was a man named Ribbentrop who became very popular in the western world but who was later hanged at Nuremberg. We have seen those beguiling smiles before. Has anyone forgotten the words of that completely sincere prime minister of Britain who, returning from Berchtes-gaden, said he believed that Hitler had no aggressive aims? As he got off the plane from that famous and tragic trip he used the words "Peace in our time".

Let us not forget that comparatively recent history. Let those of us who lived through that period of Hitler make sure that the younger generation, who were not even alive at that time, remember the similarity to some of these events. That was the period when the second world war could have been prevented. We have that statement on the authority of the greatest statesman of modern times, if not of all time, namely Sir Winston Churchill. If the western nations had stood firm on that occasion-not denying any evidence of friendship that might be extended but standing firm in their own faith and conviction and not forgetting the dreadful realities that were there-there might have been no second world war.

speechtext: I am not saying anything about that, but I do want to say I was a member of the government and heard the report when Mr. King returned here and that was not the report.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This would not be the first time during this session when the minister has been extremely wrong in the statements he has made.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

I was not questioning the
earnestness of the prime minister of Canada on that occasion, and the right hon. gentleman who has interrupted me twice should not be so sensitive. I did not know he accepted any responsibility for it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

That is one of the most encouraging things that has happened during this session. It is a refreshing change. We want to hear the truth as well, and we want to hear accurate statements from ministers opposite, which we have been getting on very few occasions since this session began.
The Budget-Mr. Drew
Again I come back to the fact that on this occasion I was merely illustrating that men who were earnest, men who sought to interpret events with the hope of peace in their minds, were beguiled. All I am suggesting is that we be warned by what happened on that occasion, and what happened to the government of which the minister was a member, because he remembers how hopelessly unprepared this country was as a result of their folly.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is exactly why I am calling my hon. friend's attention to the statement he made a few moments ago. It is not correct. The statement which was made here at the time suggested had to do with trying to get a sufficient amount through this house to make proper defence possible.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is a pity that nobody carried out that intention, because it was not done. The fact is, as the minister should know if he does not know, that no steps were taken at that time to prepare effectively for the war which many people saw coming. It will be recalled that at that time so convinced was the government of which the minister was a member that there was not going to be a war that they would not even let the R.A.F. train in Canada in preparation for a possible war.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

I wish now, Mr. Speaker, to deal with a subject that is very closely related to the subject I have been discussing, as has been illustrated by some of the interruptions which have been made. I refer now to a figure in the budget. It has been said by many that this budget contains nothing worthy of comment. In some ways that is true. There are, however, one or two things that are worthy of comment and that demand comment. One of them is the truly remarkable figure of $1,775 million for national defence, exactly the same figure as last year. This figure speaks for itself. Nothing more clearly reveals the utter bankruptcy of initiative in this government than to place a figure in the budget which everyone recognizes is given without any attempt to examine the requirements of national defence carefully.
It is not possible that we would have exactly the same figure if there had been any attempt of any kind to examine this subject. In fact I do not believe there is an hon. member opposite, even including the Minister of Agriculture, who would assert that this represents a considered opinion in regard to the requirements of national defence. It is simply a figure taken out of the blue. It is simply a figure that says in effect, so far as the Minister of Finance is concerned, "Well, with a crowd like this what is the use anyway?" He found he was not able to get any assistance from his colleagues, so he just put in exactly the same figure.
A figure of that kind invites extravagance. It is put in without any attempt to examine the changes that have been taking place. Where is the evidence of the changes that have taken place both in the United States and Great Britain in regard to the organization of defence units? Surely every hon. member saw a description a few days ago of the organization of airborne divisions in the United States. This is something we have been urging now for several years. It is something we have been urging as the rational approach in Canada to the problems of national defence.
Why is it that every senior officer who has been free to speak has criticized our military organization? I certainly do not agree with everything that has been said in those criticisms. I certainly do not agree with some of the proposals that have been made. But it is significant that senior officers who have been charged with the secret responsibility of dealing with our defence forces, when they have gained their freedom to speak have indicated their dissatisfaction with the organization as it now exists. We Canadians for


years have criticized the fact that, excellent though our permanent force may be-and it is-the bulwark of defence in Canada is the militia, the volunteer forces in the air force and navy. It is there that the great pool of manpower and womanpower is created. There is not an hon. member in this house with any contact whatever with the militia forces at this time who does not know that our militia is hopelessly unequipped and unprepared. Any hon. member who does not know should examine what the situation is in regard to armour, in regard to artillery, in regard to other equipment of that kind. In spite of all the money we have been spending the militia is not in a position to mobilize if that dreadful necessity should come. When the first world war broke out it was possible to mobilize in Canada. When the second world war broke out it was possible to mobilize. Today it would not be possible to mobilize the militia; yet we are spending these vast sums of money.
I asked that this subject be referred to the committee on estimates. I wrote to the Prime Minister asking that this be the first subject to be placed before the committee on estimates. That was not done. This is the second year this unsatisfactory experiment is being carried out by a truncated committee with no powers; but with great care the government is avoiding bringing before the committee the one subject that should come before it with highest priority. This cynical figure, exactly the same figure as last year, makes it clear that there should be such an examination. I would not want this subject to be referred to a committee which has no teeth, the committee on estimates which has been denied any effective power.
There is, however, a way in which the Prime Minister could give this house some evidence that the government is really anxious to tackle the national defence problem. We have several standing committees of this house. Those committees deal with various subjects. The standing committees now set up are:	the standing committee on privileges and elections; the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines; the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills; the standing committee on banking and commerce; the standing committee on public accounts; the standing committee on agriculture and colonization; the standing committees on marine and fisheries; mines, forests and waters; industrial relations debates and external affairs. Not one of these subjects is nearly as important as the subject of national defence.
It would have been ineffective if this subject had gone before the muzzled committee that was set up by the resolution presented by

the government. I ask the Prime Minister now to take the appropriate steps to set up a standing committee on national defence, which will continue as a standing committee and deal with the responsibilities of government which account for nearly half the total expenditures, when we include all the incidental requirements of national defence. If that were done right away there would be plenty of time to bring before that standing committee experts in the various fields and find out what the facts really are; find out just how many artillery units could go into action in Canada; find out how many armoured units would be in a position to carry out any real military duties; find out what the real state of the equipment of our different militia defence units really is at this time.
Such a committee also could call before it the senior officers who are now free to speak. It would be much more useful for them to speak before such a committee than at the various places they are now speaking. I am not criticizing the speeches they are making. I do suggest, however, that the place where their statements would be most useful would be in a standing committee such as I have suggested. From such a standing committee, a committee similar to those we have in regard to much less important subjects, we could have constructive proposals which undoubtedly would result in tremendous savings in many lines, and probably increased expenditures on some of the technical equipment that is required.
Certainly one of the things that could be done would be to examine into this question of an entirely airborne army able to move in a matter of hours to any part of Canada or any part of the world. That is no longer a visionary thing; it is a reality, an airborne army in which the infantry, the artillery, the armour, the engineers and all the ancillary units are carried by aircraft to the points where they may be needed. Suppose, for the sake of argument, that paratroops were dropped in some of the distant areas of our northland. How much use would some of the static units be that we are now training? At any rate, let that be examined; let the whole organization be examined. And I repeat, in the face of the obvious need for such an inquiry, in the face of that cynical figure, the exact figure used last year without any change, I urge the Prime Minister to give evidence to this house and to the people of Canada that the government really desires to organize our national defence for the effective protection of this country.
Now I wish to deal with something else that is not entirely unrelated to that subject. One of the most interesting developments in the United States in the last couple of years has been the extent to which oil and gas
67509-176i
The Budget-Mr. Drew pipe lines have been recognized as part of the general program of national defence. The present budget makes it clear that in spite of the bland assurances we have received from the always optimistic and usually inaccurate Minister of Trade and Commerce, there is no expectation at all on the part of this government that the eastern section of the pipe line to eastern Canada will be started this year.
The fact is that there is no clear policy of any kind in regard to this subject. There is no clear policy as to what is to be done in regard to these enormous resources of gas now available, as well as oil. This government has been dilly-dallying in a confused and hopeless manner with a vitally important subject because of the fact that they have committed themselves to a particular gentleman who obtained a franchise from this government. It is true that the interests have been extended in recent times.
This is a subject in regard to which there should be some policy. This is a time when it would be appropriate that such a policy be announced. We read in the papers about interviews that have taken place between a gentleman named McMahon and the government in regard to possible pipe lines. We, of course, only know what the papers tell us. We are merely members of parliament. It is the usual way we find out the facts. That is usually where the government gives the information that should be given here. There are suggestions that there have been other discussions. We do not know. At least we should have at this time some statement of policy in regard to this matter.
I suggested at the very beginning of this session that this question be referred to a committee. I pointed out that it could be referred to one of the standing committees and the facts obtained in regard to this very important subject. There are many places in Canada where pipe lines will be built. Already one is being constructed over the Rockies to the western coast. There has been much talk of one to come east, and undoubtedly other pipe lines will be built.
This is a subject which should be explored and in regard to which the house should be fully informed. The government should discuss this subject with the railways of Canada instead of helplessly saying there is only one way in which this can be done. Let the government explore the possibilities; let it see' what the railways can do. They have rights of way now. We are told about the difficulties which exist in northern Ontario. Well, long years ago those difficulties were overcome by a free enterprise railway with the assistance of Sir John A. Macdonald and his associates in the government of that day.

The Budget-Mr. Drew
The very fact that the difficulties were overcome has some bearing on the immediate problem. We all know from flying over that area that there are many lakes and rivers and many jutting hills in the north which make it a difficult area through which to create new rights of way for railways or for any other purpose. Why not explore the possibility of taking advantage of the rights of way that have already been established by the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways across that northern Ontario stretch?
There is nothing visionary about this; it has already been done elsewhere. In the United States the Southern Pacific Railway has done that very thing. It formed a subsidiary company and last year it built an oil pipe line which was completed in January of this year. It is not a small pipe line. It is 1,500 miles long and extends from the refineries at Los Angeles east to Phoenix, Arizona and to the military fields in that area; then it proceeds from there to Tucson, Arizona. The greater part of that oil pipe line is within the actual right of way on both sides of the rail line of the Southern Pacific Railway. At some points where sharp contours suggest the advantage of short cuts the line cuts away from the right of way, but generally it follows the right of way.
The Southern Pacific Railway has not stopped there. Through its subsidiary it has now projected the construction of a further pipe line eastward from the refineries around San Francisco bay to Reno and on to an airbase at Salon, Nevada. That pipe line is about 700 miles long, making a total pipe line operation of about 2,200 miles built by a subsidiary of the Southern Pacific Railway. This subsidiary is a common carrier. The oil companies in the area served by that common carrier avail themselves of the facilities, and then the oil is sold in the east and distributed by the ordinary distributing organizations.
I merely put this forward, Mr. Speaker, as an indication of what can be done. This has been done elsewhere. The reasons for doing it in the United States are not nearly as great as they are in Canada, where it is costly to create new rights of way through difficult areas. There is no essential difference between oil and gas pipe lines. This is something that should be explored immediately. We know that Alberta has vast quantities of natural gas; Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec want that gas. This is the time for action.
I have already pointed out that the minister told us in this house only ten months ago that he did not like the method, the third method, that was then being considered. I refer to the third method, the one which is now before


us. I ask the Prime Minister once again to tell us why he now accepts the method he did not like, and I urge him to see that without delay the government examines what is being done in the United States and examines the possibility of getting our own railway companies to co-operate in this matter in order to have our pipe lines controlled by Canadians for the benefit of Canadians.
What happier augury could there be for the future development of these great services than to have those rights of way which were created with such hardship many years ago in the days of Sir John A. Macdonald provide the opportunities for the new common carrier at this time. This is something that would challenge the imagination of every Canadian. It is something that would make is possible to get ahead with this proposal which has been delayed for far too long. We want to see pipe lines built in this country. We want to see Alberta gas used in the east and in the west. We want to see it used to the greatest possible advantage of this country.
I want to speak about another subject which appears in the budget and which certainly should not be ignored, and that is the truly unique proposal in regard to the taxation of certain magazines in Canada. In his remarks the Minister of Finance asked us what it would be like to contemplate the possibility of having no Canadian magazines expressing Canadian thoughts on Canadian subjects. Without putting this on a personal level I think I can say that no member of this house has been more vocal than I, either in this chamber or outside it, about the need for truly Canadian thought and the development of a real Canadian culture upon a natural and sensible basis.
Perhaps it is not inappropriate if I recall that I have been a fairly extensive contributor to Canadian magazines on different occasions, and for that reason I have some personal knowledge of this subject and some personal interest in the extension of the facilities offered in this field. I believe there is a great need in Canada for a far greater emphasis on Canadian achievement at this time than is possible under the circumstances that exist today. I believe those Canadian magazines that are serving Canada are doing a splendid job. I think they deserve great credit because they are carrying on their task under great difficulty. Nevertheless any one of us who goes into any book store finds the shelves filled with reading material of a nature that I could not describe in terms which would be permitted in this house. It is material which is destructive, which serves no useful purpose. Certainly if the government is going to try to tackle this problem I

think it might well tackle it at that point. Some of these filthy documents that come in, some of these crime comics and things of that kind, might well call for attention by the government in any greater emphasis that may be placed on Canadian achievement.
I noticed just a few days ago in one of the publications with a very large circulation that comes in here-I imagine the same statement was repeated in advertisements in others- that Captain Eddie Rickenbacker was the ace of aces. Captain Rickenbacker is now president of Eastern Air Lines and is a most admirable and courageous gentleman who deserves full recognition for the part he played in the United States air force in world war I. However, it is perhaps not inappropriate for Canadians, especially young Canadians, to remember that there were at least 15 Canadian pilots who shot down more German aircraft in the first world war than Captain Eddie Rickenbacker.
The official figures given out at that time were that he had shot down 21 aircraft, but I notice the figure in this advertisement is 26 aircraft. I do not quarrel with that change, but I would recall-and this is something young Canadians might well recall, not to glorify war but to show the stuff of which our young people are made, those who lived at that time and those who are with us now- that in the first war, when aircraft for the first time in history took part, the greatest pilot in the western armies was Colonel Billy Bishop, who shot down 72 aircraft. Not far behind him was Colonel Colli-shaw who shot down 61, and not far behind him was one of the most gallant airmen who ever lived, Captain Billy Barker, who shot down six German aircraft in one day. Only two behind him was a gentleman whom I like to remember at this time. Just as Eddie Rickenbacker is still serving development in the air as president of Eastern Air Lines, we have as executive assistant of Trans-Canada Air Lines a most gallant gentleman in the person of Group Captain MacLaren, who shot down 48 German aircraft and six German balloons. He is still doing a magnificent job day by day serving Canada in its civil air development.
I want to see these things kept alive by all means. Let us give men like Captain Eddie Rickenbacker full credit, but let us remember something of what our own people have done. Let us remind our own youth what they have done in the first war, in the second war and in the days of peace as well. I want to see that done. I want to see Canadian magazines serve Canadians; I want to see Canadian publications serve Canadians; I want to see Canadians assert their own position in every field. I only wish this government were nearly as
The Budget-Mr. Drew solicitous about some other aspects of the Canadian economy as they purport to be about Canadian magazines on this occasion.
The desire to have a truly Canadian expression of opinion, a truly Canadian recording of our own history for our own use, does not justify a discriminatory tax of the kind which is now proposed and which is without precedent in this or any other jurisdiction. I must say that I would like to know who really is the father of this unnatural child. I do not believe that the Minister of Finance conceived this strange offspring.
It is strange that this proposal should be put forward by this government, extremely strange. In an effort to encourage Canadian magazines the Bennett government imposed a uniform tax on all foreign magazines coming into Canada. It is a late day now to argue whether that was right or wrong. It was done, and it was this government that repealed that tax. Whether or not that was the best method, at' least it was a uniform and not a discriminatory tax. If this government have some better method let them produce it, but do not let' them bring in this strange thing which is half-baked, impracticable and completely unsound as a method of taxation.
However, there is one particular reason why this government finds itself in a strange position when asserting this principle. I hope the Prime Minister will speak on this particular subject. I hope the Prime Minister will tell us why the government which professed such concern about any taxation on magazines now imposes a tax of this kind. There is a special reason why I would like to hear from the Prime Minister as to why they have imposed this tax. Nothing shows better what a completely half-baked idea this is than the action of the government itself in regard to television. The government tells us that it is concerned about any possibility of Canadian thought and culture not being disseminated through Canadian channels, but what is this government doing with television and radio? This is something which involves Canadian ideas, Canadian writers, Canadian workers and Canadian culture.
If this government believes in dealing with this problem let it start with its own organization which it controls, and controls so rigidly. The C.B.C., which is directed by this government so carefully, buys United States programs which involve the employment of writers in the United States, of actors in the United States, of news commentators in the United States, of stage hands in the United States, of musicians in the United States, and of all those who are engaged in what we call entertainment and culture.
The C.B.C. buys these programs with money put up by the Canadian taxpayer. It

The Budget-Mr. Drew buys some of these as live programs and it buys some of these in film form. This government which is so concerned about magazines buys these before they even know who the advertisers are. It buys such programs as will be helpful to Canadian culture as "I Love Lucy", "The Honeymooners", "Mama", "Father Knows Best", "Studio One", "Disneyland", "The Ed Sullivan Show" and a score of others in the same category. I do not know under what rule of Canadian culture these programs are bought by the chosen instrument of this government, but they are bought and then sold to Canadian advertisers. Canadian advertisers sustain these United States actors, writers, stage hands, musicians and others working on these programs who deny Canadians the possibility of presenting programs that might have been shown. The Canadian taxpayer, of course, puts up the money.
It is an interesting thing. They go far beyond anything contemplated by the magazines. They subsidize these United States programs. They are not even satisfied to deny the principle they assert with regard to magazines. They not only buy these programs and then tell advertisers what they can have and for how long, but they sell these programs for an average of 40 per cent less than they pay the United States producers for them. The Canadian taxpayer puts up that money. That 40 per cent is part of the budget now before us. That 40 per cent is part of what this government does to protect Canadian performers, writers, actors and others. Oh, of course I should not forget that the live shows are brought in by the microwave relay maintained by the Canadian taxpayer. They could not be brought in in any other way. That does not appear as a special item in the budget.
This government which expresses such concern and decides that we are going to be 20 per cent Canadians, this government through its own agency is putting up Canadian taxpayers' money to make perfectly sure that at least half our programs in this country will be created in the United States, employing Americans in the process.

Before I leave this subject let me also deal with the statement made by the Minister of Finance that because these magazines were really dumped here, having been paid for first in the mass media market of the United States, they were able to sell their advertising cheaper. May I point out that this statement is entirely incorrect. I have here the advertising figures based upon the latest rate cards issued by the different magazines. These are the advertising rates


for full pages per 1,000 circulation and are as follows: Time magazine, $7.44; Maclean's, $5.97; New Liberty, $4.95; Weekend, $3.69; Star Weekly, $4.16 and Chatelaine, $6.34. It will be seen that Time magazine charges the highest line rate per 1,000 editions for a full page advertisement.
I think we should also realize that the Canadian magazines have a large circulation and are not without opportunities to express their opinions. Time has a circulation of 170,000 in Canada. Reader's Digest, with its English and French editions, has a circulation of 900,000. But these are the circulations of the Canadian magazines: Star Weekly, 913,000; Weekend, 1,400,000; Maclean's, 510,000; New Liberty, 500,000 and Chatelaine, 400,000. As a Canadian I am very glad that there are these large circulations. I want to see these circulations maintained. I want to see Canadian programs maintained on television and radio. I want to see Canadian ideas distributed in every way. That will be done by other methods than this weird and hybrid form of taxation which has now been placed before us.
There is a real problem here, Mr. Speaker. I think there will be common agreement with the general purpose of widening as much as possible the dissemination of Canadian ideas. I hope the government will reconsider its position in regard to this particular proposal. Before the government does anything of this kind let it start by putting its own house in order. Let the government through its own agency encourage Canadian programs. Let the government make it quite clear to its agency that, at any rate, it is not going to subsidize United States programs with the Canadian taxpayers' money. Let it encourage, in the reasonable ways it can, Canadian writers, Canadian artists, Canadian performers, Canadian musicians.
Today in this field the government is the worst offender. On the basis of the assertion made by the Minister of Finance it is to be hoped there will be immediate action to deal with this problem. Let us, however, deal with the problem as a whole. We still have three or four months before this session will be over. Let this problem be brought before the members of the house in such a way that it can be examined detached from the budget. In the meantime, on the basis of its own preposterous action with regard to television, let the government in common sense drop this discriminatory and impractical tax, start all over again and for once seek the assistance of the members of the house in solving this very important problem.
I said that the government should seek the assistance of the members of the house. It is time it did. For long years great concern

has been expressed about the diminishing authority of parliament and the way in which the government is taking unto itself the business that we are sent here to do on behalf of the people of Canada. This government treats parliament with contempt. What should be remembered is that we are merely the people's representatives. The government is treating the people of Canada with contempt. It is denying not to us but to the people of Canada whom we represent, information which should be available to every one of us.
Let me give a recent example of the kind of answers this government gives. I had hoped that when the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Balcom) spoke yesterday he might have mentioned this. Just before the Easter adjournment he asked this question, as found at page 2587 of Hansard:
What industries have been organized and are operating in Nova Scotia since 1951, through the assistance of the small industries division of defence production-
This is the answer of the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe), and a typical answer it is:
The small industries division of the Department of Defence Production was created in 1951 to ensure that all segments of Canadian industry, particularly small industry, were given an opportunity to participate in the defence production program. Its chief function was that of a service division, to assist and advise those firms seeking either direct contracts from the Department of Defence Production or subcontracts from the department's prime contractors. In order to accomplish this, the small industries division until 1953 maintained representatives at various locations across Canada, including a representative in the maritime provinces who assisted a number of Nova Scotia contractors in the manner above outlined.

Mr. Speaker, that is not from "Alice in Wonderland". That is from the records of this house. That is the answer given to a question as to what industries have been organized and are operating in Nova Scotia since 1951, through the assistance of the small industries division of defence production. This government carries secrecy to the point of a mania. It is secretive when there is no reason for secretiveness. What earthly reason was there for a vague, uninformative and meaningless statement of that kind in answer to a perfectly clear question? The answer probably is that they have done nothing. Why did they not say so? But this is a typical answer.
This is something that has been under discussion for a long time. I go back to the year 1909, a long time ago. On that occasion Sir Robert Borden, then the leader of the opposition, is reported in volume I of Hansard of that year at column 368 as follows. I just
The Budget-Mr. Drew wish to quote a few words because they indicate the concern felt then:
We hear a great deal, both in the United States and in Canada, of the decadence of our legislative institutions, the decadence of the influence of parliament, in these latter days, when almost all the work of government is confined to the members of the cabinet.
I wonder what Sir Robert Borden would have said if he had been confronted with the disregard of parliament that has been shown throughout the whole of this session? I think he would have exploded. Can anyone imagine what Mr. Mackenzie King would have said if he had been denied information in the way in which we have been denied it? As a matter of fact, he said a few things, and this was one of them. I quote from page 36 of Hansard of 1935 what he said in the House of Commons on January 21, 1935:
I have said that one of the supreme efforts of this administration has been stealthily to alienate the authority and control of parliament, to take power into its own hands and away from parliament with respect to many of the important affairs of the nation.
Mr. Speaker, at that time no one would have dared do what this government now does. They did not set up a committee from which they had first drawn all the teeth so it could not even masticate the problems that came before it. They did not set up committees which were only propaganda agencies for well-prepared representatives of the government to put over their fancy ideas when the committees met.
I can imagine what would have been said by Mr. King if anything had been attempted such as was attempted here. I ask those members who still recall his assertions on behalf of a free parliament what he would have said if he had been confronted with some of the things that have been done in this parliament, such as the falsifying of Hansard by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner); the inaccurate answers of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson); the ignorance of his own department shown by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney); the reckless disregard of the facts-I am keeping within the rules, Mr. Speaker-displayed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) who over and over again talked about an order in council of July 7, who chided my friend the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) when he forgot that important fact, and who did not of his own volition tell the house that there was no order in council. Let us remember that. The only reason he told us there was no order in council was that I had asked the Prime Minister to produce that order in council and he had agreed to do so. Then,

The Budget-Mr. Drew and only then, the Minister of Trade and Commerce had to admit that there was no order in council.
Mr. Speaker, there were times when governments would not have tolerated answers of that kind. The Prime Minister has the highest measure of responsibility under our system. He is asked by the representative of the crown to form a government, and he is responsible for the conduct of the whole government. He has not acted upon conduct which would have called for extremely stern measures in other parliamentary bodies which operate under methods similar to our own.
May I remind you again of words spoken by his predecessor as far back as June 30, 1920. I refer to the Hansard record, at page 4540 of that day. This is what was said by the man to whom the present Prime Minister has paid such great tribute:
The business of the country should be carried on in the open on the floor of this parliament in such a manner that the government will be obliged to take into their confidence not only the members of parliament but the people of the country whose money they are voting to expend.
Mr. Speaker, with whatever disagreement any member of this house may express his opinion with regard to some things that were said by the predecessor of the present Prime Minister, let it be said that those words clearly expressed what the attitude should be to the people's representatives here in parliament. The business of this country should be carried on in the open. I would ask you to remember that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill), when asked a question about the Caughnawaga reserve which he did not want to answer, made the pretence that he wanted a debate on the subject and availed himself of the rules in order to achieve that result.

But I would point out that if there has been any delay in dealing with the business of this house, it has been the result of all the confusion that has been created by this government in the handling of the business of the house, and by the deliberate evasion of the responsibilities of the government to this house. No worse example could be offered than that which was presented by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the proposal to set up a committee to examine into the role of government in the field of non-military research in Canada, including operations in the field of atomic energy, and the operations of the national research council.
That motion stood on the order paper from the beginning of the session. It came before this house- on February 24, six weeks ago. That is an important committee. The motion was debated for one day and then was dropped. It is difficult to believe that there was any sincerity whatever behind the government's proposal that this committee should be set up. How does the government explain holding back the discussion of that motion? It was difficult to explain why they waited until February 24, but how do they explain holding this matter up now? It was up for discussion for one day and then it stood on the order paper. We now enter the second stage of this session and the time is extremely short within which this subject could be dealt with, even if this motion were brought forward and passed this week. I am reminded that it was up briefly a second time, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce became impatient and the debate did not go on very long.

speechtext:
It is my purpose to congratulate him most heartily on the report he brought down for the financial year which has just ended. As you will remember, Mr. Speaker, a year ago the Minister of Finance, after introducing substantial reductions in tax rates, forecast a deficit of some $160 million. A week or two ago he was able to tell us that deficit had been cut by more than two-thirds to $52 million, a very gratifying result, I think, and the more so because of the substantial reductions in tax rates last year.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the budget speech and the white paper which accompanied it showed us very clearly the flourishing condition of the Canadian economy as a whole, a condition which I think must be a source of pride and satisfaction to all of us in Canada. The gross national product for 1955 reached the figure of $26-5 billion, a real increase because as we know there was no appreciable change in price levels. This gross national product was 10 per cent above that of 1954, and perhaps even more significant was 9 per cent above the peak year of 1953. Yet all of us, Mr. Speaker, recall that last year when the Minister of Finance forecast a gross national product of $26 billion, his estimate was derided by the opposition as fantastically optimistic. We can all remember that dismal chorus of gloomy prognostications which sounded like a dirge from the prophets of woe sitting on the opposition benches.
But what has happened? The minister's estimate of the gross national product has been exceeded. He has confounded his critics;
10, 1956
The Budget-Mr. A. M. Fraser and his confidence, and the government's confidence, in the boundless resources of this country, in the skill and energy of the people of this country, has been completely vindicated. This rise in gross national product, Mr. Speaker, was reflected in increased employment. As the white paper states, the national average of employed persons in 1955 was 5,328,000, a 2-5 per cent increase over 1954 and 1-5 per cent increase over 1953. What I think is particularly important, Mr. Speaker, is that this increase was a steady increase. It was higher than in 1954 in every month except January, and higher month by month from May onward than even 1953. This increase in employment was accompanied by an increase in wages, salaries and supplementary labour income in 1955 which reached the magnificent total of $12,861 million, an increase of $872 million or 7 per cent over 1954.
There was unfortunately, as the house knows, a fall in farm cash income of $55 million in 1955. However, apart from that single exception of farm income, all forms of income increased. There was an increase in interest, dividends and net rental income from $1,825 million in 1954 to $2,010 million in 1955, a rise of $185 million or 10 per cent. There was a rise in net income of non-farm unincorporated business from $1,645 million to $1,753 million, a rise of $108 million or 6 per cent, and in corporation profits from $2,420 million to $3 billion or 24 per cent.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make reference to a statement made by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) during the course of his speech. He stated, as recorded on page 2568 of Hansard for March 23, 1956:
There Is rather a striking contrast between the increase of 7 per cent that was added to labour income and the increase of 20 per cent that was added to investment income.
Of course that is quite true, but what the hon. member did not point out is what seems to me a very significant and relevant fact, namely that this large increase in investment income in 1955 came after several years of little or no increase in the level of investment income, while labour income increased steadily in every one of those years. As a matter of fact corporate profits, by far the largest factor in corporate income, actually decreased in 1952, 1953 and 1954. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, even if we take investment income as a whole we will find that in 1953 it increased by less than 1 per cent over 1952, while labour income increased by 7-7 per cent. Again in 1954, investment income was slightly less than for 1953, about a quarter of 1 per cent less to be precise, while labour income increased by 2 * 4 per cent.
