Taking the period 1952-1955 as a whole, therefore, we find that investment income was 18-8 per cent higher in 1955 than it had been in 1952, while labour income was 18-3 per cent higher in 1955 than in 1952. In other words the rate of increase in investment income from 1952 to 1955 was only one-half of
I	per cent higher than the rate of increase in labour income over the whole of that period. This, I think, gives a very different picture from the one presented by the hon. member for Nanaimo, and I submit a very significant one.
The substantial increase in incomes to which I have just referred placed greater purchasing power in the hands of the Canadian people and made possible a higher level of personal expenditures. This reached the record figure of $16,811 million, an increase of 6| per cent. And here, Mr. Speaker, I think it is -especially gratifying to note that the rate of increase was particularly large in expenditures on durables, which rose by
II	per cent as compared with 6 per cent on non-durables and 6| per cent on services. Undoubtedly, personal expenditure was at a peak in the last year.
Savings also reached a very high ievel, showing an increase in personal savings of $500 million, more than 5 per cent over 1954, and in gross business savings another $500 million, more than 16 per cent over 1954. Yet, Mr. Speaker, despite this phenomenal expansion, there is no reason to suppose the limit of Canada's growth is reached. As a matter of fact, the minister's estimate for the gross national product in 1956 is close to $28 billion, and I have heard no opposition member claim that that figure is too high. That is a very different picture from the gloomy one that was painted last year by the opposition.
On the basis of an estimate of gross national product close to $28 billion, the Minister of Finance has budgeted, as we know, for a revenue of $4,775 million. With expenditures at $4,650 million, he estimates a surplus of $125 million. We have heard criticism from the opposition on the ground that with the increase in the gross national product and the surplus in prospect there should have been a large reduction in the rates of taxation. I feel they are fundamentally mistaken, but first of all, before I go on to analyse that question further, I should like to remind the house that there have been cuts in the tax rates, small ones, it is true, but they have been very wisely applied to those sectors of the economy where they will be most helpful. I have in mind in particular the repeal of the sales tax on building materials, providing as it does an encouragement to home builders, and the


restoration of full duty-free entry to parts for agricultural machinery and equipment, which will be of benefit to our farmers.
Now, Mr. Speaker, to get back to the question of the criticism on the ground that there has not been a larger reduction in the rates of taxation, we all know, of course, that there are only three ways in which it is possible to reduce taxes. Either we must reduce expenditures or abolish the surplus, or the minister could have budgeted for a deficit. Let us consider each of these possibilities in turn. There have been very strenuous general demands by the opposition for a reduction in expenditure; but I have read all the speeches in this debate very carefully, Mr. Speaker. I have listened to a good many of them and I failed to hear any specific concrete proposals from the opposition that would have resulted in substantial reductions in expenditures. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, during this session, as in previous sessions, we have heard from the opposition side of the house demands made for increased expenditures that would have involved the imposition of higher taxes by many millions of dollars upon the people of this country if they had been accepted by the government. Therefore, until the opposition comes forward with specific practical proposals for a reduction in expenditures that would make possible substantial reductions in the rates of taxes, I can only conclude that the Minister of Finance is completely justified in the fiscal course he is pursuing.
Suppose the minister had not budgeted for a surplus, what then? Could there have been substantial tax cuts? Well, no, because of course the surplus is too small. It is only $125 million, and as the minister himself has pointed out, that represents only about 2\ per cent of our revenue or expenditure. If I may quote the minister: "It is not much more than a prudent reserve against unforeseen circumstances that may arise in the course of the year". Moreover, we must bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that during the past two years the public debt has been increased by $153 million in 1954-55 and by $52 million in the last fiscal year, 1955-56. Consequently, if it does prove that this estimated surplus materializes it could be usefully applied to a reduction of the public debt.
It should not be forgotten, however, Mr. Speaker, that there is a likelihood of substantial additional expenditures to be faced by the government in 1957-58. I think particularly in the first place of the proposed nationwide health plan which has been estimated to cost the federal treasury about $180 million annually, and also the proposed new federal-provincial tax arrangements,

The Budget-Mr. Nesbitt refer. I should like to express my strong support for the government's decision to increase Canada's contribution to the Colombo plan, an increase of $8 million or 23 per cent. I believe that this is a particularly wise decision in view of the fact that at the present time the cold war is being waged more and more by economic weapons and in the economic field. I support this decision both because I believe it is inspired by a genuine desire on the part of the government to help the economically undeveloped countries of the commonwealth and Asia to help themselves and also because I am quite confident that in doing this the government is doing what the overwhelming majority of the Canadian people would have it do. I believe, too, that the Colombo plan is serving as a model of the best way in which aid can be offered to countries whom we want so much to develop their resources and to do so in an atmosphere of good will and with no strings attached.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would just like to say once again how much I appreciate the soundness and the statesmanship which has lain behind the administration of the finances of this country during the past year, and to congratulate the minister once more on the extremely sound budget which he has presented to this house for its adoption.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the Minister of Finance did not see fit in his budget this year to institute a major change in financial policy it is with regret, I think, that many hon. [DOT] members view the fact that he did not remove certain small inequities in the present taxation system. While the inequities are not very important in themselves, a change would have brought inestimable relief to many individuals in the country. For example, a farmer who is a widower or a bachelor might have been allowed a deduction from his taxable income of a reasonable sum paid for the services of a housekeeper. This may be a small point, Mr. Speaker, but on the other hand there are many farmers in that particular category, and dairy farmers in particular have not shared in the boom which the rest of the economy has been enjoying. A farmer is not in the same position as an industrial worker who lives in an apartment in the city. Although it is not an essential part of the farming business a farmer must maintain a home. If the farmer has a child a certain type of deduction may be allowed if he is a widower and the child acts as housekeeper, but if the farmer's children have grown up or if he is a bachelor he has no relief in this way. It would seem to me that a minor form of relief such as this might easily be put into effect.


Another area in which I think the minister might have given some relief is with regard to the education and training of blind children. At the present time special training for blind children is not allowed as a deduction from taxable income for those who supply the funds for such training. I am sure it would make very little difference to the gross income which the minister obtains for carrying out the business of the country if a deduction such as this were allowed. It is a terrible handicap for one to be blind, particularly from birth, and considering the relatively small number of blind children it seems only reasonable that their parents who must put up the funds for their training should be given every conceivable assistance and aid in this matter.
There is another matter which I mentioned in this house last year and which I shall continue to mention from time to time as the opportunity presents itself. I refer to the cost of expensive drugs not being allowed as a deduction from taxable income. Lengthy illnesses are almost always very expensive and there are many families in the lower income groups who are not members of the Blue Cross or other health schemes. In many cases the drugs required for the treatment of these lengthy illnesses are exceedingly expensive.
As most hon. members know, in some cases the physician will supply the necessary drugs and then charge for them on his account to the patient. Then under the exemption for medical expenses over 3 per cent the taxpayer is able to deduct the cost of such drugs from his taxable income. This method discriminates directly against the druggists in the country. The druggist makes his livelihood from dispensing prescriptions and selling drugs. He provides a necessary service which should not be supplied by doctors. However, many doctors do provide this service in order that their patients may take advantage of deducting the cost of drugs from their taxable income.
I realize that there are certain administrative problems in allowing as a deduction from taxable income the cost of such drugs. I have heard it said that people would go to a drug store and get a receipt when they buy toothpaste, cosmetics, cigarettes or anything else. I am quite sure that this relatively minor administrative problem could be easily overcome by having the druggist set out on his account what was purchased. When the bills were attached to the income tax form it would be quite easy to see whether cosmetics had been purchased instead of drugs.
I mention this because many druggists throughout the country are incensed with

the present regulation. I received many letters last year after I made my remarks in the house in this connection and I know the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) has received representations from druggists' associations. It apparently is too late this year but perhaps next year the minister will consider allowing the cost of such drugs as a deduction from taxable income. It is an unwarranted discrimination against druggists which could be easily overcome.
There is another matter to which I should like to refer briefly before I reach the main object of my remarks today. I might say that on another occasion I intended to deal with this matter in greater detail and much more fully. I refer to the excessive-this is the only possible way to describe it-tax on tobacco which exists at the present time. I have always been led to believe that in its taxation policy the government follows the principle of ability to pay, and I think most groups in this country subscribe to that principle. However, it is quite obvious that that principle has not been applied to the tax on tobacco.
In the old days tobacco may have been considered as a luxury. It was largely imported and there may have been some excuse for applying a tax. But today tobacco is not a luxury. Whether people like it or not, it has become what could be described as an economic necessity. A large majority of the people in Canada, particularly those in the lower income groups, use tobacco daily as they use bread and other things. It is the low income groups that are hit by this excessively high tax.
It does not seem fair. We have often heard that the government should soak the rich, but in this case they are soaking the poor. In view of the generally high level of taxation, this tax on a commodity which is used largely by those in the lower income groups seems to be most unfair and unreasonable. It is shown by figures and charts which I have before me that because of the high tax on tobacco the per capita consumption of cigarettes in this country is somewhat lower than it is in the United States where the tax is less. As a result there is not the maximum use of tobacco that there ordinarily would be.
This has resulted in a reduced tobaccogrowing acreage, which in turn has resulted in considerable land in southern Ontario, land which is of no use except for the growing of tobacco, becoming waste, sandy land. You find this condition in the counties of Oxford, Norfolk, Brant, Northumberland, Simcoe and elsewhere.
I know that some objections to the reduction of the tax on tobacco may be put forward on health grounds, but it has never
Private Bills
been shown conclusively that tobacco has any adverse effect on health. Many members of the medical profession say that it has, but just about as many say that it has not. Until we have conclusive figures I do not think that the government should attempt to use health, if it is doing that, as an excuse for putting a tax on tobacco. If the government can produce medical evidence that the use of tobacco has an adverse effect upon health, then possibly some other measures might be taken, but they should not be in the form of an excessive tax.

speechtext:
It being five o'clock, the house will proceed to consideration of private and public bills.
PRIVATE BILLS	'

The house resumed, from Monday, March-26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lefranqois for the second reading of Bill No. 160, respecting Personal Finance Company of Canada, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Coldwell.

Mr. Speaker, because of the rather disjointed manner in which this discussion of this bill has taken place, it might be wise for me at the outset of my remarks to remind the house that this bill calls for a change in the name of the Personal Finance Company to Beneficial Finance Company and also for an increase in capitalization. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has moved an amendment that the bill be given what we commonly call a six months hoist.
A continuation of this debate may come as a surprise to some hon. members of the house because it has been obvious to me as I have listened to the debate that some hon. members are inclined to regard this as a rather innocuous bill which should not concern us particularly. This, Mr. Speaker, gives me cause to realize that more than ever it is necessary for those of us in the house who believe in the things about which the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) spoke yesterday to rise in our places and draw to the attention of the house that as far as we are concerned this is not an innocuous little piece of private legislation but rather is a case in point of the very things about which the hon. member for Cape Breton South talked in the house yesterday afternoon. It is a present-day manifestation of the kind of attitude of mind that exists in this country which caused the people who drafted the Regina manifesto, to which the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Carrick) re-

Private Bills
ferred, to say that they would not rest content until capitalism had been eradicated from this country.
In rising to oppose the passage of the bill I want to make it very clear that that is the basic reason for my doing so. The very fact that in some quarters the bill should be considered to be an innocuous matter, something to which little heed or attention should be given, the very fact that a company should come to the parliament of Canada and ask us in effect to prostitute the English language is not something which we should sit idly by and see happen. In attempting to make my position clear I should like to point out that the writers of the Regina manifesto did not say they were going to eradicate capitalists from Canada. However, they were determined that this state of mind, this attitude which considers the almighty dollar the most important thing in the life of man, should be brought to an end, and that they would seek to build in this country a cooperative commonwealth.
It is perfectly true that the people who have attempted to warp and twist that statement, drafted at a time which most of us can recall was one that wrung the hearts and minds of men in the agony of the situation that existed, have attempted to suggest that the plan there set forth was one which would eliminate private enterprise. That is the sort of approach which is taken by people who will bring this kind of bill before the house, a bill that is helping to eliminate private enterprise and initiative in any real sense in this country.
That is why I feel I want to take part in the debate today in opposition to the passage of this measure. Why should I be concerned about what a particular company calls itself? As it happens, this is a matter that comes before parliament, and this company is asking that it be allowed to term itself "beneficial". I happen to believe that this company and its operations are not beneficial to the people of Canada and that it is an affront to us for the company to come here at this time and ask us to give our blessing to this change.
A while ago I took the trouble to look at a dictionary to see what the definition of the word "beneficial" is. I found that "beneficial" means benefiting, tending to benefit, conferring benefits, being helpful. The Beneficial Finance Company may be beneficial to some people but in my humble opinion it is a long way from being beneficial to the people who are unfortunate enough to do business with it.
I have discovered that many people in Canada get rather a jolt at times when they happen to find out the kind of mark-up that the merchants with whom they do business place on the products they sell. They may

hear that there is a mark-up of 25 per cent on certain goods they buy, or they may happen to discover that in some cases their hardware merchant may have a mark-up of 100 per cent on his goods, and they are shocked to the core. I wonder how many of them have stopped to think about the kind of mark-up this company has. I wonder how many members of the house have thought about that.
According to the company's own statement, which can be found in the report of the superintendent of insurance, I notice that under the heading of small loans they list under expenditures interest on borrowed money amounting to $642,231.28. To me that represents the wholesale cost of the commodity they are selling. Then, above that item under the heading of income earned on small loans there is an amount of $2,769,313.25 listed. I think a rough calculation will indicate that represents a mark-up of something over 500 per cent.
How can anyone, Mr. Speaker, term that a legitimate kind of business? Certainly as far as I am concerned I make no bones about my opinion of it. I noticed an announcement in the press recently that this particular company is opening an office in the Alberni valley where I live. As far as I am concerned, I certainly intend to advise my constituents to avoid that particular business like the plague, irrespective of whether or not the name of the company is changed. In my opinion there is no justification for the continuance of this form of legalized robbery. Because of the existence of this sort of institution, which attempts to fasten itself upon the backs of the working people of the country, there is, as far as I am concerned, still need for a party like the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation which is dedicated to the eradication of this kind of capitalism.
It is perfectly true that the operations of such companies are glossed over a little more smoothly now than back in the thirties. These people have discovered the benefit of having high-paid press agents to do their dirty work for them. In my opinion some of these press agents have warped the judgment of a good many members of the house over the course of the years. As far as I am concerned, this is an attitude of mind which represents the greatest enemy to the well-being of the people of Canada today.
It is all very well for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) to talk about our bounding economy and the increase in our gross national product. Surely, we can slide along under that. It is perfectly true that some of the grosser effects of this kind of activity are glossed over in a period such as that in which we live at the present time. But that does not

alter the fact that still fastened like leeches on the backs of the Canadian working people is this sort of thing, the people who do the really productive work of this country. Probably the people who are in the position of being entrepreneurs in the genuine sense of that term do not have to resort to the use of this sort of lending institution. But unfortunately the people who work under their direction, beguiled by this misleading and high-priced publicity that is bombarded upon us from every direction, have resorted in large numbers to the use of this sort of thing perhaps partly because in many instances they have not been fully aware that it was unnecessary that they do so. When I think of the contrast in the approach that is taken by an institution of this kind with its 500 per cent mark-ups to the kind of service which is provided to many Canadians today through their credit union organizations, Mr. Speaker, I think that I am on even surer ground in rising in opposition to this measure.
If no other alternative was available it might be argued that, little as one liked this sort of thing, it was necessary and that we should give our blessing to their calling themselves "beneficial" or anything else that they might see fit to call themselves. But when there is in existence the kind of lending institution which is beneficial in the genuine sense of the word then, as I said before, I think the proposal contained in this bill constitutes in effect a prostitution of the English language and that we should have neither hide nor hair of it.
The other aspect of this particular piece of legislation is this. If we grant this particular proposal to this company, are we not in effect creating a precedent and are we not going to have all the loan companies and many other companies coming running to this parliament asking to be allowed to change their names in a manner which may give them, in their opinion, some slight competitive advantage over their competitors in misleading the public of this country? We are perhaps going to have coming in bills proposing all sorts of changes of names and we shall be spending our days and our weeks dealing with such bills.
I was wondering just what sort of names some of these other companies might want to have if they were to come in with similar bills. Again I consulted a dictionary in order to see what were some of the synonyms of the word "beneficial". I could offer a few helpful suggestions to the people who might be coming in with these bills. They might call themselves the "advantageous" finance company, the "good" or the "helpful" finance company or-I do not quite know how this one got in-the "profitable" finance company.
Private Bills
I might even support a bill for a change of name to that one. Then, of course, Mr. Speaker, there is another synonym. They might call themselves the "salubrious" finance company. I think that name somehow has a rather nice sound. If the Personal Finance Company, instead of making this particular proposal, would agree to a change and would come in and ask us to give them the name of the "salubrious" finance company I think possibly I might withdraw some of my objections to their proposal.
Quite apart from this particular consideration, Mr. Speaker, I am reminded of remarks made earlier in this debate by, I believe, the hon. member for Trinity in which he tried to shoo us off and say that he thought this was not the time and the place to debate this question, that we could debate it on the government legislation to change the evil ways of finance companies when we came to it. That is all very well and good, Mr. Speaker, but my contention is this. After this government legislation to which he is referring has passed and has gone through the house, if we are satisfied that it is going to do something to rectify the situation and to make a decent, ordinary type of business out of this activity, we might be prepared to consider some proposal such as this. But until we know what is going to happen with regard to that legislation or what is going to come out of the discussion on it in this house, I submit that now is the time and place to debate this bill, and no other time. After all, the bill is before us under the rules of the house. If we feel that it is an evil and pernicious thing to be coming before us I would suggest, Mr. Speaker,-with all respect to the hon. member for Trinity-that this is the time and the place to debate a measure of this kind. I could only hope that the people who direct this company, after taking some cognizance of the objections we have raised, might be willing to have this particular legislation withdrawn, at least in so far as this proposed change of name is concerned.
There are too many ways in which this insidious abuse of the English language is creeping into the accepted ways of doing business in an attempt to extract every last nickel and dollar from the working people of Canada. Here is a flagrant example of it that has come directly before us. It is, if you like, an example symptomatic of an attitude of mind that is all too prevalent among those who consider themselves to be in the business world of this country. It is something we should oppose. Actually, Mr. Speaker, it is something which has nothing, to do with what are ordinarily termed divi-

Private Bills
sions in thinking along political party lines. So far as I am concerned, it is something which goes much deeper than that.
It is based upon a recognition of the truth of the statement that man does not live by bread alone. Day after day, year after year, possibly because of the period of prosperity which was induced by and has continued since the last war, this type of thinking seems to be more and more accepted as something to be taken for granted; something which we can casually accept as part of our way of life. So far as I am concerned, this sort of thing is something which, if we hope to retain our freedom as individuals, we have to stand up and fight against. Otherwise, we are going to be lulled into a state of semicoma-perhaps a state of coma which is a little deeper would be a good thing. In such a state, Mr. Speaker, we would not feel the pain when these financial dentists are pulling our financial teeth. It is an intriguing thought, that we just allow ourselves to be lulled into a gentle somnolence, and let these financial wizards continue extracting everything we can earn.
I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that man was intended to spend his life sleeping on a doormat. I think the people of Canada, if they are going to remain people, have to be alive to the fact that there are some things that hurt. If one is aware that one is being robbed, that does hurt. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I think this bill should be thrown out. I feel that when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) moved that this bill be not now read but be read this day six months hence, he was taking an action which was designed for the welfare of the Canadian people. This house would be well advised, as a parliament charged with matters pertaining to the welfare of the Canadian people, to accept the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.

We
are considering Bill No. 160, Mr. Speaker, and I think when one is talking about this bill one should probably recall that we are dealing with two bills, No. 160 and No. 166. I think one could make a distinction as to how one feels about these two bills, and that is what I propose to do today. I will say at this stage, although I realize I am not discussing Bill No. 166, I will vote against that bill and I will vote for Bill No. 160. The reason I am willing to vote for that bill is that I think we are dealing with pure technicalities.
We understand that the Personal Finance Company wants to change its name to the Beneficial Finance Company. In my opinion, *that is not important. I do not like the name. I do not think it makes sense particularly, and

I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett). It is a rather silly name, but actually it is their own business. They are operating as a company in this country. They are obeying the laws of the country, and so far as I can see there is no reason why, on a pure technicality, they should not be allowed to change the name of the company.
Now, about two weeks ago the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Carrick) pointed out that this name has met with the approval of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard) and the approval of the superintendent of insurance. If that is the case, I do not think it is incumbent upon hon. members, in effect by means of a filibuster, to try to block something which is purely a technicality. It seems to me that this is not a matter of substance. It is a matter of procedure. It is a matter of dealing with the name of a company only and not a matter of dealing with the merits or demerits of small loan companies. Hon. members well know how I feel about finance companies. I mentioned it in a speech I made just a few weeks ago. I believe that when one is considering such a company as the Signature Loan and Finance Company, that is an altogether different matter. There you are dealing with powers which are vested in hon. members, namely the decision as to whether or not a new company should be set up in this country.
It may well be, and it is my own opinion, that this is not the proper time for another company, particularly a United States company, to come into this country and especially when one receives letters from people who are concerned about the future status of Canadian finance companies. But surely in a matter which purely concerns the name of a company that is already in existence, which is operating in this country and which, so far as hon. members are aware, is obeying the laws of this country, we members should not interfere with this purely technical process. As I say, I cannot see that it concerns the merits or demerits of finance companies generally. Hon. members well know that soon Bill No. 51 will be going before the banking and commerce committee. At that time evidence will be adduced as to whether or not the interest rate should be changed. Personally, I feel it should be, and I am strongly in support of the government bill. But, Mr. Speaker, I submit that is not the case here. Therefore, as I say, I will support this bill but I will speak, and I will vote, against the subsequent Bill No. 166.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Except that it is rather beneficial to the Beneficial Company.

Mr. Speaker, I should like at the outset to congratulate the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth), who has just taken his seat, on the statement he has made that at least he intends to oppose one of these bills.
I think that is a noteworthy admission for him to make, and I hope that the national president of the Liberal party will not deal overly harshly with him when next the Liberals nominate in York Centre.
Various names for this company were offered by my colleague, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett). I think he left out two other possible names. One might be the MacTavish Finance Company. After all, this man, Mr. MacTavish, is connected with a goodly number of these companies and he might well consider it is high time that his name was honoured in the name of one of the companies; or it could also be called the National Liberal Finance Company. That, Mr. Speaker, I think would make it have a very salutary effect both upon the Liberal party of Canada and upon the welfare of the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Why not call it the C.C.F. Finance Company?
The name of the C.C.F. finance company is known in almost every village now as a local credit union, and they are doing very well.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: That is about the only enterprise of the C.C.F. that did not go bankrupt.
The hon. member does not know what he is talking about.

I think, Mr. Speaker, that the C.C.F. or the credit union method of helping people shows that people can be helped with small loans at reasonable rates of interest.
Private Bills
I should like to compare just for a moment the attitude taken toward this bill by the newspapers belonging to the millionaires of Canada and the more moderate newspaper published in Ottawa. The Financial Times- that is the one I am referring to as a millionaire newspaper-in its issue of Friday, April 6, begins under the heading:
The C.C.F. and the Small Loans Companies
Unsuccessiul in their attempts to have the interest rate on small loans cut in half, the C.C.F. members of parliament had an opportunity of renewing their attacks on small loan companies in the course of debate on a bill providing for a change in name for one of the companies operating in the small loans field in Canada.
I must point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that that is a complete misrepresentation of the facts. The C.C.F. has not been unsuccessful. As I pointed out in another debate, the introduction of another bill by the government shows how successful we have been in our attacks in regard to what is going on in the field of finance companies. The other paper, the Ottawa Journal, was much more realistic. On Wednesday, March 28, over and above the news item headed: "D. K. MacTavish Attacked Over Loan Firm Connection", they have a very interesting cartoon. A man and his wife are washing a new automobile in the shade of a tree, and they look at a man walking in the dusty road, and the comment is:
A finance company put him back on his feet. They took his car away from him.
I think that is a very good example of the different reaction of the ordinary citizens of Canada, as exemplified by such a newspaper of a relatively smaller city, as compared with that taken by such a newspaper as the Financial Times. The one opens up with a completely false assertion. It is as false an assertion as were the assertions by the man named "Tempus" in the same issue of the paper when he attempted to forecast the number of seats the various parties would win in the province of Saskatchewan in the next' federal election. He was wrong in that. I am rather surprised that the wealthy people of Canada have only such unreliable newspapers to read.
The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Car-rick) made some very interesting comments on this bill the other day. He rightfully pointed out that this bill not only implies a change of name but also asks us to authorize an increase in the capitalization of the company. He asked at page 2618 of Hansard:
Does that not seem a reasonable request?
Does it not seem a reasonable request that this company be allowed to increase its capitalization from $1 million to $10 million? When speaking on this bill, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Maedonnell) rather

Private Bills
wondered whether the increase in capitalization would mean that the company would be prepared to put in an extra $9 million of their own money. In looking at the financial statement of this company, Mr. Speaker, I think it is obvious that it wants to raise its capitalization from $1 to $10 million merely so that it can issue share certificates for the surplus $9 million odd that they now have. I would like to suggest that since their net earnings under the Small Loans Act are roughly $1 million, they feel that $1 million net profit on $1 million of capitalization would indicate a net return of 100 per cent of their money in one year. They feel that they could raise the capitalization to $10 million without investing any more money, and that then in another year a profit of $1 million will look like only a mere modest 10 per cent earnings on their investment.
The question of the propriety of our entering the debate at this time has been raised by a number of speakers, both by the hon. member for Trinity and again by the hon. member for York Centre. I feel that when a company asks for an increase in its capitalization it has always been considered quite the appropriate time for parliament fully to examine the operations of the company that is asking for such an increase. If we look at the operations of this company we find some very interesting statistics. First of all, the company admits that in the year ended December 31, 1954, it spent on advertising the sum of $473,991.70, a little less than half of it on small loans, and the rest of the money was spent on loans in excess of $500. I feel that is imposing an undue hardship on the Canadian people. I do not think this advertising of theirs served any useful purpose whatsoever. If it is an emergency service they are rendering, I am sure the Canadian people are aware of telephone directories, and they can look up and find out where finance companies have their offices. No money whatsoever need properly be spent on advertising. If the advertising would lead to some competition among those companies I might be willing to consider it in a more favourable light. However, you find that the interest rates are fairly well the same. You can go from one to the other and it is 2 per cent a month on the unpaid monthly balance.
I am also interested in two things. My leader, in moving his amendment to the bill, read out the list of the directors. However,
I would like to call attention to the fact that the largest shareholder, of course, by far, is the Beneficial Loan Corporation of Wilmington, Delaware, but there are two other citizens of the United States on the board of directors. There is a Mr. O. W. Casperson, of Andover, New Jersey, and Mr. C. H. Watts, Fort

Lauderdale, Florida. I have reason to believe that both Mr. Casperson and Mr. Watts are the men who own the Beneficial Loan Corporation, so there is a very clear indication there that this is a company almost completely controlled by outside interests.
The hon. member for Trinity had the audacity to compare the usefulness of this company and its American money with the Aluminum Company of Canada. On page 2620 of Hansard he makes the statement that in so far as the earnings of both companies go to the United States, because the Aluminum Company of Canada is a subsidiary, there is not a scrap of difference. I would like to take issue with that statement. To me there is a very great difference. If the surplus earnings of the Aluminum Company of Canada are taken out of Canada and go to the United States we at least have the satisfaction of knowing that this company has aided in the development of our natural resources. That is something which we definitely cannot say concerning the operation of finance companies. The purchasing power of any money they take out of Canada is definitely lost to the Canadian people and the standard of living of the average Canadian citizen is lowered in ratio with the millions of dollars they take out of the country.
The hon. member for Trinity concluded his remarks by saying that the relief sought is reasonable. I feel that asking parliament for the right to use a name which in fact can be most misleading to the Canadian public at large and the request to increase capitalization when it is obvious that no additional investment on the part of the company is contemplated is in no way reasonable.
At page 2619 of Hansard the hon. member for Trinity gave expression to a remarkable thought when he said:
I put this question squarely to hon. members of this house. Is the choice of a name going to depend upon the likes, the dislikes or the whims of members of this house?
That comes about as close to contempt of the rights of parliament as anything I have yet heard any hon. member here express.
I can only say that this is a further indication that the speech was written in the ante-room of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), because if I did not know that that sentence had been used by the hon. member for Trinity I could readily believe it was a sentence the Minister of Trade and Commerce had used.
The hon. member is a great joker.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce has frequently expressed contempt

for the rights and responsibilities of hon. members of the House of Commons. I feel that to mislead the people of Canada with a proposed new name is definitely a matter that concerns this parliament and when we are asked to sanction such a change of name I believe we have every right and responsibility to consider its implications in full.
I notice that the operations of these companies indicate that these are vicious activities indeed. I have not the figures for the Personal Finance Company of Canada in detail on the matter I now wish to raise, but in looking at page 59 of the report of the small loan companies and money lenders for the year ending December 31, 1954, I see under the consolidated exhibits a classification of loans made during the year. It divides the borrowers into three categories: new, repeat and current. "New" means persons who were not previously borrowers from the lender; "repeat" means persons who had fully discharged all previous loans from the lender; "current" means persons with earlier loans from the lender still undischarged.
I notice that a total of 831,721 loans were made in the year and of this figure over half, or 484,667 people, were borrowers who when they came in to borrow were still indebted to the finance company for some loan made previously. This should be a warning to the people of Canada that of the total number of Canadians who found themselves in the clutches of finance companies over one-half were unable to get out of their clutches and found themselves deeper and deeper in debt.
When you hear that the veterans of Canada are paying as much as 8 per cent of their income to finance companies, I think it is time we gave some serious consideration to what is taking place.
That was for interest alone.

The hon. member for Assiniboia has corrected me. He says that the 8 per cent figure is for interest alone, which makes it that much worse.
There were a few matters in the financial statement to which I would like to call the attention of the house. This company, which pays 25 per cent as much on advertising as it pays in wages, is also to be condemned for the level of wages it pays. The Financial Times appears to point out that the men who run these offices must be wise, must be able to help people and advise them how to spend their money and therefore they assume that the employees are very well paid. I happen to know that the employees of finance companies in Canada are paid on a scale that is put to shame by even the miserable wages paid by the chartered banks.
Private Bills
You can pick up a newspaper almost any day of the week and look under the help wanted column where you will see that some finance company or other is continuously advertising for help, especially male help. They lure male employees with the prospect of becoming branch managers. At the rapid rate at which they are opening branches I suppose there are a considerable number of vacancies from time to time; however, I have reason to believe that a large number of their branch managers receive only mediocre wages and therefore they resign with regularity and the turnover in employees is very high.
The main complaint I have against the Personal Finance Company is that it, like other finance companies, is using money that is not its own. It is bleeding the people of Canada for the use of their savings. Many hundreds of thousands of Canadians who have money in the bank or in life insurance companies and receive the measly percentage of interest on their investments must pay the exorbitant interest rates that are being charged by finance companies when they buy automobiles and household appliances. I feel that no one should be allowed to manipulate the savings of the Canadian people in this fashion. Under the heading "liabilities" I notice that this company owes to the Beneficial Loan Corporation the sum of $31,757,529.68. Apparently the reputation of the Personal Finance Company is so low that it cannot borrow from Canadian banks or insurance companies but has to persuade the parent company to do its borrowing for it.
I resent very much the change of name and I resent the increase in capitalization that is being asked for, because I feel it is only misleading in that no additional capital will be forthcoming.
I repeat that the people of Canada should know, and I hope they soon will know, that the Liberal party of Canada is intertwined and intermeshed in this plot to collect the hard-earned savings of the Canadian people which is going on at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I intend to point out one of the newer things in which we find these small loans companies engaged. I refer to the rather nefarious expansion of their present practices and I rise to draw this to the attention of the house at this time.
Before I do so I should like to point out something known to a great many members of this house, especially those who have had anything to do with the credit union movement. Credit unions are engaged in exactly the same type of operation as these small loan companies which we are discussing and yet the interest rate charged in most instances

Private Bills
is only 8 per cent and the borrower is insured so that if he dies the loan will not be charged against his estate. Then in most instances a good part of the interest paid is returned in the form of dividends. We are familiar with the operations of small loans in the credit union movement. When we are told, as we were told here a day or two ago, that the exorbitant interest rates charged are due to the risk involved and the cost of processing loans, we know that will not stand up when the facts are presented.
I should like to point out a new practice which has been established in this country by these loan companies. They are not able to get all the business as there are many other institutions such as department stores which are getting a tremendous amount of business because so many people indulge in instalment buying. Even in the city of Ottawa we see the insidious practice where subsidiaries of these small loan companies are set up. They go to people who have become financially embarrassed, to people who find their pay cheques too small to meet their monthly commitments to the department stores, to people who are unable to make their cheques go around; these subsidiaries which are operated under other names but which are exactly the same people go to these people and say, "If you will turn over your pay cheque every month we will take care of your obligations around town." They charge 2 per cent for that service.
After they have operated for a few months they come back to the party and say, "Because of our handling of your accounts we are able now to allow you to make a down payment on another piece of merchandise." I do not think it takes a great deal of imagination to realize exactly what is taking place. It has been proved in this house that Simpsons-Sears and T. Eaton are charging as high as 52 and 54 per cent on instalment buying. These people in effect are collecting, not 26 per cent-

speechtext:
Order. I hesitate to interrupt any hon. member who has the floor but I have been listening to the hon. member for the last three or four minutes and I find it a little difficult to connect his remarks with the present bill. As hon. members know, there is a general bill dealing with small loan companies now before the banking and commerce committee. There are only two clauses in the bill now before us. I have no desire whatever to hamper the hon. member in making his argument, but I think I should ask him to deal with the specific bill before the house.

Mr. Speaker, I understand your position but the reason I was pointing this out is that I feel we must reject this legislation because of certain principles in which we believe. I was pointing out my arguments as to why we should not tolerate in this house the establishment of these small loan companies, regardless of what they may be called. However, you have made your point quite clear and I shall not press the matter further.
I do not think we can accept the argument which has been put forth by the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth), who said that it was immaterial at this time whether the name was "Beneficial" or not. I submit that if we agreed to changing the name to "Beneficial" we would thereby be agreeing to the operating of such organizations.

That is a non sequitur if I ever heard one; it does not necessarily follow at all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening
I intend to spend the rest of my time dealing with the dairy industry. Of course, it is quite impossible in 20 minutes or half an

hour to even begin to deal with all the problems of the dairy industry in any detail and with any accuracy. Consequently I intend to deal with two aspects of those problems, the problems that the cheese producers and the concentrated milk producers face at the present time. Without any exaggeration I think that these two problems are the most contentious problems at the present time of the many difficulties that the dairy farmers face.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, one must bear in mind that all branches of the dairy industry are very intimately related. In fact, they are rather like a pile of jackstraws. If you remove one of the straws the whole pile shifts. Consequently, if one branch of the dairy industry benefits or suffers all other branches benefit or suffer accordingly. I think hon. members should bear that in mind with relation to the rest of my remarks.
People regard the function of government in the world at the present time from two different points of view. If one is a socialist one considers the function of government to be that of the all powerful arbiter of the factors of production. Government decides where the various factors of production, land, labour, capital and management are to go, what products are to be produced and what products are good for the people. Those who subscribe to that theory consider that to be the function of government, but for those who believe in a free enterprise economy, a free economy, as some put it, the general function of government is somewhat different.
I think it may be safely said that in a free economy it is economically and socially desirable for the government of any nation to preserve a balance between groups; between farmers, labour groups, professional classes and so on who are in competition for a share of the national income. It is also true that many times in the past governments in this country have acted to protect or strengthen different groups within the nation. For example, tariffs have been established to protect new industries or industries which are essential to a balanced development of our country, industries which have to compete with lower cost industrial competitors or agricultural competitors from the United States or elsewhere.
Subsidies have also been used to maintain this balance. For instance, at the present time $2 per capita for every man, woman and child in Canada is used to subsidize those who are unemployed in the form of unemployment insurance, and about $1 per capita is used to subsidize the gold mines. However, when you get to the dairy industry
The Budget-Mr. Nesbitt you find that in the years from 1949 to 1954 an average of about 3 cents per capita has been used to help that industry. One might almost say that the government had forgotten the dairy industry with certain exceptions such as the 58 cent floor price on butter.
Agriculture as a whole in Canada has not shared in the general prosperity. It has not shared in the big boom we have been enjoying largely because we are so closely connected with the United States economy. Dairy farmers in Ontario in particular have profited from this boom the least of all. From 1951 to 1953 the net income of Ontario dairy farmers declined 25 per cent. In 1954 it declined another 12 per cent with a probable further decline in 1955 and in the present year, 1956. Unfortunately I do not have those figures yet.
It must be remembered that Ontario produces 48 per cent of all dairy products in Canada, and Quebec is a very close second. In 1954 agriculture's share of the national income was 6-8 per cent, the smallest since 1931. The situation of the small share of the national income has been aggravated very much by the increased requirements for farm capital outlay, increased production costs and the increase in costs because of the higher standard of living generally. Needless to say, a prosperous dairy industry is essential in Canada in peacetime and in war, whether it be a hot war or a cold war. Seventeen per cent of Canada's population is involved in the dairy industry, with a production in 1954 of somewhat over $900 million.
Farm groups have become increasingly concerned about this problem. The dairy farmers of Canada, the dairy farming association and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture have asked for tariff increases on cheese and skim milk powder. Of course, as hon. members know, and the minister particularly, the question of tariffs is very complicated indeed. In theory free trade is, of course, perhaps the ideal situation in the world in that the principle of natural advantage can be allowed to run the gamut. With the exception of non-economic reasons such as defence and so on, this might be the ideal situation.
However, we are not dealing with the world of theoretical economists but with the world as it exists for better or for worse today. Free trade is not feasible in the world today for many reasons. As hon. members know, there are wide wage differences and differentials in standards of living between one country and another. Then there are exchange restrictions, quotas and so on. Large well established industries in Canada such as the dairy industry and certain manufacturing industries must be protected. If they have been well established and have been in exist-
2800	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Nesbitt ence for a long time and a situation arises where they are threatened they must be protected or the whole economy becomes dislocated. This, of course, applies particularly to anti-dumping tariffs. I think the situation with respect to tariffs has been put reasonably and sensibly by one of my colleagues in the house, the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair). I should like to refer to Hansard of April 27, 1954, page 4176, where he had this to say:
I do not believe it is advantageous to the economy of this nation nor do I advocate a high protective tariff policy for this or any other industry-
The hon. member was referring to the dairy industry at that time.
-because such a device can only provide stability for an uneconomic unit at unwarranted high cost to the Canadian consumer of the products which the industry produces.
Farther on in the same speech and on the same page the hon. member went on to say:
As far as tariffs are concerned, they should not be so low as to cause failures of efficiently operated Canadian businesses, nor so high that inefficient producers could still remain in business.
I am quite aware, Mr. Speaker, that Canada is a member of the general agreement on tariffs and trade, and I do not think there is a member of the house who would quarrel in any way with the general principles of GATT. Unfortunately, however, many of the member countries have not always lived up to the agreement, and our large neighbour to the south is one of them. I am not necessarily stating this by way of criticism of those countries that have done that because sometimes when a general rule is laid down exceptions arise to which attention must be paid. In dealing with economics or anything else in this world it is very difficult to lay down a hard and fast rule. Eventually situations arise when changes have to be made in some cases. When the economy of a country is threatened by conditions that were not foreseen at the time agreements were entered into changes may have to be made.
Let us look at the situation regarding cheese and skim milk powder. The present tariff on skim milk powder is as follows. As far as British commonwealth countries are concerned, it is 2J cents a pound. The mostfavoured-nation tariff is 5 cents a pound. The general tariff for other countries is 5 cents a pound, except-and here is the important part-that Australia and New Zealand have a special tariff of only 1 cent a pound on both cheese and skim milk powder. This tariff was instituted by the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, when he was prime minister of this country in 1932, by a special tariff agreement with New Zealand and Australia. I see some hon. members opposite and I can gather what may

The Budget-Mr. Beaudry insurance, gold mines and other things. This would place approximately $2 million more per year in the hands oi dairy farmers and would be $2 million more in purchasing power for farm implements and supplies; $2 million towards keeping the industry in Canada; $2 million that would help the dairy farmer and avoid the necessity for depleting his capital.
In closing, I should like to point out one other thing. The Ontario cheese producers association have done a remarkable job in marketing their own produce by means of a stabilization fund. It has been suggested by many leaders of the dairy industry that a similar plan be put into operation for the whole of the dairy industry. I contend that any "self-help" plan run by an association such as this is much better than any government board set up to do the same thing. There is a genuine desire to sell under a "self-help" scheme. No such scheme as this, however, could be effective or would be worth-while unless the dairy industry is protected against the importation of New Zealand cheese and skim milk powder. I think it is very nearly time the government considered putting a tariff on these items and caught up with the times.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my first duty in rising tonight is that of thanking providence for restoring my health, and in the same breath thanking those of my colleagues who were so generous in their sympathy and understanding over a long period of more than two years. This little wing seems to be dedicated to what my late friend, the great Louis Francoeur, would have described as "the passionate pursuit of the fly speck".

speechtext: These joint leaders, Mr. Speaker, are tireless in their pursuit of the miserable fly speck. They have no peers at the lowest altitudes and their range is limitless, although if I may borrow from the vernacular of aeronautics, they usually seem to fly by the seat of their pants. The measure of their courage-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-their vision, their concept of statesmanship is best assayed by their contempt for the higher issues. They prefer to deal in human equations, to trade in human frailties. They stand up in this house as the knights of the picayune. Oftentimes, their concern for the safeguard of the nation's interest forces these gallant knights to ride in different directions. The hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace is wont to ride, galloping, in search of wall-eyed reindeer. The hon. member for Quebec West has no less zeal but less ambition. He has drawn to himself the somewhat lower duties of counting house attendance and members' bar chits. They ride fearlessly, their lances tilted to the ground, the better to scavenge, the better to display their infinite genius which is a genius for the small and low things. Woe to him who does not meet their standards of human assessment. Their wrath is soon spoken.
Now, the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace has acquired to his escutcheon other bars. He wields his scalpel not only on the living, but under his valorous hand it becomes a dissector of the dead-even for them, he shows no respect. These are but a few of his glorious achievements in statesmanship.
In less time than it takes to say Bill Hamilton, he has burst the bubble of legend and tradition under which the gentlemen who have sat in this house for over 80 years have conducted the affairs of this country. Under his leadership, this house has learned that the confidential perusal of confidential papers no longer imposes on one the duty of respecting confidences. In one fell swoop of his shining scimitar this valiant knight has severed the bonds which, honour imposed, spring from mutual trust and respect, and by which this parliament has been guided ever since Sir John. I have a premonition, Mr. Speaker, that given another year or so we shall come back to these standards. No one will suffer, least of all the Conservative party. But that is enough, I think, about him. We should deal with matters beyond his scope and come to the budget.
Thrift is frequently a virtue, perhaps always. However, it offers a pitfall here and there. I should like to bring one to the attention of three ministers, perhaps more.

The ministers concerned are the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe). We on this side of the house have long held to the theory and practice that government purchases by tenders should be made from the lowest tenderer whenever he offers the required guarantee of performance. I have no quarrel with this practice and its application, and I am well satisfied that it best serves the interests of the Canadian taxpayer in most cases. I would, however, like to take issue with the application of the principle in cases, infrequent I grant, where it does not best serve the interests of the country. And broadly, this applies to cases where all tenderers for the sale of a given commodity offer no supplies of Canadian origin, but are importers of such supplies from any of the group of different countries, some of which undergo different treatment in respect of import duties.
The specific case I have in mind does not deal with large amounts of money; it deals with the purchase of musical instruments for the armed forces, most of the instruments purchased being of necessity of foreign manufacture. The concrete result is that by purchasing from the lowest tenderer as against a slightly higher tenderer the saving effected thereby is sometimes smaller than the income which would be derived from the duty which the higher tenderer would have to pay to import his goods into Canada.
I have some specific facts and figures on a group of tenders. I refer to tender B-20 A-l-642, March 30, 1954, where a low tenderer offered units at $146 and where a high tenderer offered goods at $163. We purchased from the low tenderer, as was normal. However, in effecting our purchase we overlooked the fact that the goods purchased at $146 had entered Canada duty-free, whereas the goods which would have been purchased at $163 had entered Canada after paying a duty and a sales tax amounting to $20.10, so that if this country had purchased from the higher tenderer we would have saved $3.10 for each unit purchased.
I will not bore the house, Mr. Speaker, with further examples, but I would say this. I would suggest to the three ministers concerned-and there may be others-that in any such cases we should not be necessarily guided by the almost inexorable law to purchase from the lowest tenderer, but perhaps by exceptional practices to first determine the true eventual dollar profit to the national exchequer. I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, and I fully apologize to the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace and the hon. member for Quebec West for discussing such a topic in
The Budget-Mr. Beaudry this house before them, so far removed from their usual topics that I am almost embarrassed in bringing it up.
To come back for a moment to that virtuous nimrod, the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, that intrepid knight who looks a stamp in the eye before he licks it, that fearless discloser of confidential information, that gallant slighter of those we honour in their death, let me say this to him: Leadership is an attribute, it is not a cognomen of a man for desire or personal ambition. It is an achievement for which there is no stepping stone other than-
